text: POLITICIANS FORCED TO LEAVE?

label: text
text: "STRIKING TERROR."

label: text
text:
H.K. University Honours Man
"On Leave."

label: text
text: (From Our Own Correspondent.)

label: text
text: This morning at dawn Mr. Foo Ping-sheung, Commissioner of Foreign Affairs for Kwanqtung, followed yesterday's example of Mayor C. C. Wu, and boarded the steamer for Hongkong. his presumed destination being the international settlement at Shanghai.

label: text
text: Mr. Foo is the second prominent official of the Kuomintang Government to depart from Canton since Sunday when General Chang Kai-shek struck terror into the hearts of the "moderates" by ordering the military arrest of General Wu Te-chen, former chief of police of the city.

label: text
text: [In May, 1916 Mr. Foo Ping-sheung graduated with 1st class honours as, a Bachelor of Science (Engineering); at the Hongkong University, being the first student to do so—Ed., "China Mail".]

label: text
text: Lam Chi-fung, an assistant in the Department of Foreign Affairs, has been named acting commissioner for "the time being, and, as in the case of Dr. C. C. Wu, when news of Mr. Foo's departure is made public it will be officially said that he has gone to Shanghai for a "month's vacation."

label: text
text: As yet Canton does not know of the departure of either official, but in Government circles and on Shameen in the consulates, there is great speculation as to whether or not Chang Kai-shek will fill their places with Communists.

label: text
text: Unquestionably the arrest of Wu Te-chen, and the imminent peril which made Dr. Wu ard Mr. Fogo to Shanghai is traceable to Communist influence. Even if the Communists do not get the jobs, they seem to have General Chang Kai-shek's ear, and to have his confidence in sufficient degree to enable them to influence his mind against the anti-Communist Kuomintang officials.

label: text
text: If Mr. Sun Fo should also leave, General Chang Kai-shek would probably find himself in an unenviable position, for if the leaders of "Sun Yat-senism" are forced out of office, the loyalty of the people to Chang Kai-shek will be questionable. More than that, it is considered certain that if the Kuomintang is entirely unseated, and if General Chang Kai-shek arrogates to himself the powers of military dictator, most of the Nationalist generals now commanding' Kwangtung troops against Wu Pei-fu's allies would revolt against the local warlord.

label: text
text:
What Chang May Do.
In the latter event, General Chang Kai-shek would hold only Canton and the immediate suburbs, for his 40,000 loyal troops are practically all quartered here.

label: text
text: Additional manifestoes have been issued by the foreign office, following those concerning the ending of the Hongkong boycott and the abolition of the oil monopoly. One of the mandates appropriates $500,000 for bandit extermination, promises the people that the pirates will be cleared off from the rivers within a month, and that the land bandits will be killed or in hiding before the end of thirty days.

label: text
text:
A fourth manifesto says:—“A Labourers 'and Capitalists' Arbitration Board shall be formed, composed of an equal number of delegates, from each side, with a Government delegate as chairman, and this board shall be vested with full power to settle all disputes.”
A fifth mandate urges the people to report cases of corrupt official-dom; a sixth demands reference to the Government of all disputes between organisations; a seventh orders the arrest and trial by martial law of all reactionaries and rumour mongers; and a seventh promises reforms in matters of education and the carrying out of plans for road and harbour improvement.

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: Shanghai, June 4.

label: text
text: The students at Medhurst College, which is a London missionary institution, refused to attend service on May 30. Later they placed a heavy roller outside the principal bunces of the front door which they refused to move.

label: text
text: The students also refused to move offensive notices from the college notice board or apologise; but instead a deputation made various demands.

label: text
text: As these were not granted, the students left the college which is not expected to re-open this term. It is worthy of note that Medhurst College was not affected by last year's disturbances; but is the only college where there has been trouble this year.

label: text
text: It is also charged that since early in May, Wu, Te-chen has communicated frequently with the army, of General Lin Fu, in the East River district, and that he communicated with Wu Pei-fu's allies in Hunan and contributed to the defeat of Nationalist troops there.

label: text
text: These charges, it is understood, also involve Dr. C. C. Wu late mayor of Canton, and Mr. Foo Ping-sheung, late Commissioner of Foreign Affairs, both of whom have gone to Hongkong. Both, in public esteem, are held innocent, and the victims of plots, by the Communists who sought their exile because of the clever manner in which the Kuomintang was lately swung into line against Communism.

Vague Accusations.
The charges against Wu Te-chen, which are many, include alleged misuse and improper accounting of funds when he was chief of police, an office which he re-linquished under pressure from General Chang Kai-shek only about a month ago; and also alleged confiscation of arms belonging to the police.

label: text
text: people claim to have reports said to implicate Wu Te-chen with hiring people to set off the explosion which wrecked the Whampoa powder works last Sunday. Wu Te-chen has been succeeded as commander of the 17th Division of the Sixth Army by General Au- Yeung Kui. Arms and munitions confiscated when his home was raided are said to have been worth $40,000, and in addition he has lost more than $200,000, which he spent from his personal purse arming and equipping the Division.

label: text
text: It is now learned that secret orders had been issued for the arrest of Dr. C. C. Wu just before his departure and that Mr. Sun Fo may also go North on the pretext that he must oversee the building of the tomb of his father, at Nanking.

label: text
text: Mr. Sun Fo and Chiang Chiang-kiang yesterday waited upon General Chang Kai-shek to demand the release of Wu Te-chen, but are understood to have met with a reception far from cordial.

label: paragraph_title
text: Secret Orders.

label: text
text: General Gallent of Russia, whole left Canton for Moscow six months ago, returned here last Friday, and is now living in Tungshan. His purpose in returning to Canton is said to be to aid the soldiers of the Northern Expeditionary forces in spreading the doctrines of Communism over the territories they may conquer. He returns under direct orders of the Central Executive Committee of Soviet Russia.

label: text
text: Naval officers from provinces other than Kwangtung are now vigorously attacking the record of Poor Man-chi, commissioner of the Naval Department, and it is believed that he cannot long retain his position. Wu Hin, commander of the gunboat "Kong Koo," has finally been entirely exonerated of charges made before Commander Li Chi-lung was ousted by Chang Kai-shek early in the spring.

label: text
text: The closing rate of the dollar, n demand, to-day was 2/2.18/16. EXPOSED IN COURT.

label: text
text: Tried much too often and on a man more watchful than her former victims, a Chinese woman's tricks on rice dealers were exposed at the Central Ministry of this morning when she was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindseß with the theft of 84 catties of rice from a shop at Second Street in the western district.

label: text
text: The evidence showed that she visited the shop and asked that the bag of rice costing $7 be sent along with her to a certain address where payment would be made. The shopkeeper offered to make out a bill, but she told him this was not necessary. On the way, however, she appeared to have changed her mind and told the coolie that he had better go back and fetch the bill. Taking advantage of the man's absence, she placed the bag of rice in a ricsha and was getting away, but she had not counted on a wary foki from the shop who was watching her every move. The woman was promptly arrested when the foki gave the alarm.

label: text
text: Three other victims of similar thefts were mentioned as having identified the woman. She was sentenced to six weeks' hard labour.

text: MANY WILD RUMOURS IN CANTON.

label: text
text: PICKETS STONY SILENCE.

label: text
text: (From Our Own Correspondent.)

label: text
text: Canton, June 2.

label: text
text: Many wild rumours are in circulation here concerning an early cancellation of the boycott against Hongkong, but the pickets and_strikers maintain a_surly silence. One absurd tale has it that Hongkong is to loan Canton $40,000,000 as the price of peace.

label: text
text: The Japanese arrested on Monday on Honam on chargea of aiding Chinese to reach Hongkong have been released upon representations of the Japanese Consul General on Shameen. They were confined for nearly 24 hours in the strikers' prison.

label: text
text: Shimeen awaits with interest the arrival here from Peking of Councillor Mayer of the American Legation, who has been ordered south to investigate the long series of outrages against American citizens and American property in this part of China. He reaches Hongkong on June 10, and will come to Canton the next day.

A case is proceeding before Mr. Lindsell in which two brothers, a house boy and cook, employed at No. 67, Wong Nei Chong Road, are charged with assaulting the wash amah of the house during the absence of their employers.
Improper behaviour was alleged against the first defendant during the outlining of the case by Divisional Inspector Ogg.

label: text
text: Mr. T. L. Knight, of the American Express Company, was called to give evidence in the case. He said that he lives at an adjoining flat and on hearing a woman's screams for assistance from the back portion of the house he went there to investigate. Witness came on the first defendant and the complainant holding each other's clothing, the woman having a torn jacket and a bruised eye. The circumstances pointed to an ordinary fight.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: NAVAL SEALS BROKEN.

label: text
text: (From Our Own Correspondent.)

label: text
text: The U.S.S. "Pampanga" has returned from a trip up river to Wuchow, acting as convoy to a shipment of oil for the Standard Oil Co.

label: text
text: Conditions are reported as being quiet at Wuchow, but the Wuchow Hospital, a missionary institution, has been looted.

label: text
text: The hospital was closed a little more than a month ago as a result of strikers, picketing, and anti-foreign and anti-Christian demonstrations. When it was closed the property was sealed with seals of the American Navy, and the American Naval "Commander paid the Wuchow chief of police $300 for a special guard over hospital buildings and property.

label: text
text: On this trip, however, the "Pampanga" found the seals on the doors broken. Blankets, pillows, electric fans, many small portable articles, and one heavy and costly set of office furniture had been stolen.

label: paragraph_title
text: SALT TAX

label: text
text: FOREIGN LOANS NOT YET MENACED.

label: text
text: QUESTION IN COMMONS:

label: text
text: (Reutler's Service.)

label: text
text: The danger of the total disappearance of the machinery for the collection of the Chinese salt tax, owing to the action of the militarist leaders" was brought to the attention of the House of Commons by Mr. W. Foot Mitchell (Conservative, Saffron Walden) who suggested withdrawal from the tariff negotiations until China recognised her contracts in respect of the salt tax.

label: text
text: Mr. G. Locker-Lampson, Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, in reply, expressed the opinion that Mr. Foot Mitchell was unduly alarmed. He said that so far nothing had occurred to cause any fear that the foreign loans secured on the salt revenue were in danger of default or that the administration was about to disappear. Therefore there was no reason to withdraw from the Tariff Conference on these grounds.

text: FURNITURE BEING CARRIED AWAY

label: text
text: A strange sight presents the casual observer at the Astor House Hotel in Queen's Road Central.

label: text
text: Collies and others are marching off with furniture and odd pieces. On an application by the Chinese landlord for rent distress, the Court ordered an auction. The furniture, etc. realised nearly $4,000, part of which will pay for the back rent and the Crown rates. Business is suspended and the hall is now an idling place of furniture removers with their knick-knacks. It is stated that the place may re-open doors to the public, shortly.
